turns.t: Hello Liam, come in and grab a seat. Bit blowy out there today, isn't it?
Yeah, the wind nearly took the car door off in the car park.
Parking here is a nightmare on a Thursday. Did you find a spot alright?
Mum dropped me round the corner. She's probably circling the block right now.
Fair enough. Your mum's note says you've been wandering about at night. What's been going on?
Nothing much. I just do the sleepwalking thing. Honestly, it's not a big deal.
If you're asleep at the time, how do you even know it's happening?
Mum or my brother finds me. Standing in the hallway, or halfway into the fridge. I don't remember any of it.
How long has this been going on, would you say?
About three months, I guess.
And how often do you get one of these nights?
A couple of times a week. Sometimes less, sometimes a bit more.
What time of night do they usually turn up?
Mum reckons pretty early, an hour or two after I go to bed.
Has it ever taken you out of the house, or onto the street?
No, never. Just downstairs once, into the kitchen.
And have you ever hurt yourself, bumped into things, anything like that?
No, nothing like that. Mum says I walk round stuff better asleep than awake.
Ha, that's actually common. People steer around furniture quite well.
Right. Anyway, I think it's mostly mum who's worried, not me.
She's allowed to be. Are you taking anything at the moment, tablets, vitamins, anything like that?
Just melatonin. Mum picked it up from the chemist after the last doctor's visit.
And how much do you take, and how often?
One before bed, every night. 3 milligrams, I think? Maybe it's 5, I'd have to check the box.
Do you manage to take it every single night?
Yeah, every night. Well, most nights. I forget a couple of times a week if I'm wrecked.
Okay, thanks for being straight with me. That's useful to know.
Now, before we go any further, are there any allergies I should write down?
Yeah, penicillin, I think. Mum says I reacted to it when I was little, but I don't know what actually happened.
So you react to penicillin, but nobody remembers how.
Pretty much. It's written in the front of my health book.
Good, I'll note it. Let me check your blood pressure and pulse while you're here. Rest your arm on the desk for me.
Sure, no worries.
Blood pressure is 112 over 68, and your pulse is 64.
Is that good?
That's a nice reading for a teenager. Nothing for you to fret about there.
Cool. So what do I do about the sleepwalking?
Mostly it's about the bedroom set-up, nothing fancy. First, keep the same bedtime and wake-up time every day, weekends included.
Weekends are the best bit, though.
I know, lie-ins are tempting. Also keep the floor clear and shut the windows at night.
Mum already put a little bell on my door, which is pretty embarrassing.
Honestly, that's a smart idea. Leave it there for now.
Ha, fine. Will the melatonin fix it, d'you reckon?
Hard to promise. Let's not change anything today. Keep taking it, and try to get it in every night.
Okay. Is it going to get worse?
Plenty of teenagers grow out of these nights over time. Does it bother you much yourself?
Nah, it's just annoying for mum, mostly.
Fair enough. Here's the plan. Give the changes a good go and see how you travel.
If it's still happening in six weeks, come back and see me and we'll talk about what else we can try.
What if something happens before then?
If you ever go outside or hurt yourself, ring the clinic that same day, don't wait for the six weeks.
Okay. I'll tell mum.
Good. And you can tell her she's free to park now.
Ha, I'll text her. Thanks, doc.
Cheers, mate. Mind the wind on your way out.
